source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 1855 (untitled; numbered sections added in the 1867 edition)

source.excerpt:
I exist as I am, that is enough,
If no other in the world be aware I sit content,
And if each and all be aware I sit content.
trail: First appeared, unnumbered, in the 1855 first edition of Leaves of Grass; the poem was later divided into 52 numbered sections in the 1867 edition, per Wikipedia's overview of the poem's textual history ↗.
The exact line is preserved in the standard public-domain text of Leaves of Grass hosted by Project Gutenberg ↗.
It is also given, identically, as section 20 of “Song of Myself” by the Academy of American Poets ↗ and by the University of Iowa's WhitmanWeb ↗.
source.excerptNote: The line is usually quoted alone, but in the poem it opens a three-line stanza about not needing outside validation.

source.rightsNote: Whitman wrote in English and first published this line in Leaves of Grass in 1855, more than a century before the 1931 U.S. cutoff, so the text is in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Walt Whitman
author.heading: About Walt Whitman
author.bio: Walt Whitman self-published Leaves of Grass in 1855, a slim collection of twelve untitled poems that grew, through decades of revision, into one of the founding works of American free verse. He is remembered above all for “Song of Myself,” a sprawling first-person meditation on the body, democracy, and self-acceptance.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Section 20 of “Song of Myself” sits inside one of Whitman's recurring refrains — a refusal to seek outside approval or apologize for existing. The full stanza reads, “I exist as I am, that is enough, / If no other in the world be aware I sit content, / And if each and all be aware I sit content,” immediately followed by lines insisting the self needs no vindication.

Online, the opening clause is almost always lifted out and shared alone as a stand-alone affirmation, stripped of the two lines that originally followed it and gave it its full sense of indifference to being seen or unseen.
